questions.q: Inflation is well above 2%. What does the MPC usually do, and why?
options: Raise (or keep high) Bank Rate to cool spending and bring inflation down over time
Cut Bank Rate so people spend more
Print banknotes to pay for higher prices
Nothing: inflation always fixes itself overnight
questions.why: Higher rates make borrowing dearer and saving more rewarding, slowing spending and easing price pressure, with a delay.

questions.q: Put the effects of a Bank Rate rise in order.
items: The MPC votes to raise Bank Rate
Banks raise mortgage and loan rates
Households and firms borrow and spend less
questions.why: Rate → bank rates → spending → inflation. The last step can take a year or two.

questions.q: A £200,000 repayment mortgage over 25 years costs £1,111.66 a month at 4.5%. At 5.5% it costs £1,228.17. How much more is that a year?
questions.why: £116.51 a month × 12 = £1,398.12 a year: money that's no longer spent elsewhere.

questions.q: Which is true about the Monetary Policy Committee?
options: Nine members vote eight times a year, and the votes are published
The Prime Minister sets Bank Rate each month
It meets once a year in secret
Each bank sets its own Bank Rate
questions.why: The Bank is operationally independent; its nine-member MPC votes eight times a year and publishes minutes.

questions.q: Match each term to its meaning.
pairs: The Bank of England's main interest rate
Creating money to buy gilts and push down long-term rates
Shrinking the Bank's holdings of gilts
questions.why: Bank Rate is the main tool; QE was used when rates were near zero, and QT now reverses it.

questions.q: The Bank of England directly sets the interest rate on your savings account.
questions.why: It sets Bank Rate. Banks set their own savings and mortgage rates, influenced by it, by expectations and by competition.

questions.q: Why is the target 2% rather than 0%?
options: Falling prices can be harmful, and a little inflation leaves room to cut rates in a downturn
So that savers always lose money
questions.why: Deflation can make people delay spending and makes debts heavier; 2% gives a buffer.

questions.q: A Bank Rate rise brings inflation down within a week or two.
questions.why: The effects are long and variable: the main impact on prices often comes a year or two later.

questions.q: Why do many UK households not feel a Bank Rate rise straight away?
options: Most mortgages are fixed for two to five years and only change when the fix ends
questions.why: Fixed-rate deals delay the effect until people remortgage, which is one reason policy works slowly.

questions.q: Explain why the Bank of England, not the government, sets Bank Rate.

ideas.label: Politicians might cut rates to win votes, storing up inflation
An independent bank with a clear target is more credible, keeping inflation expectations steady

questions.model: Politicians might be tempted to cut rates before an election to boost the economy, storing up inflation for later. An independent Bank with a clear 2% target is more credible, and if people believe inflation will stay near 2%, it's easier to keep it there.

tests.answer: Politicians might cut rates to win elections, and an independent bank with a target is more credible so expectations stay steady.
So politicians can't use it to win votes.
Because the bank has more money.

questions.q: Explain how quantitative easing was meant to help the economy when Bank Rate was already near zero.

ideas.label: The Bank created money to buy gilts (government bonds)
This pushed down long-term interest rates / yields, making borrowing cheaper
Encouraging spending and investment (and lifting asset prices)

questions.model: The Bank created new money to buy gilts in huge amounts. That pushed gilt prices up and yields down, so long-term borrowing got cheaper for firms and households, and sellers moved money into other assets, encouraging spending and investment.
questions.why: QE works on long-term rates when short-term rates can't go lower.

tests.answer: The Bank created money to buy government bonds, which pushed down long-term rates and encouraged spending and investment.
The Bank bought lots of government bonds.
